## Introduction

This is the hands-on continuation of today's lecture on version control with Git.

### Learning goals for this lecture

- Learn the basic Git workflow and basic Git commands.
- Make Git ignore specific files and dirs.
- Show the changes you've made to files.
- Undo accidental changes to your files.

## One-time Git configuration

We will start with one-time personal Git configuration.
This will apply anywhere on OSC,
and won't ever have to be redone unless you want to make changes.

These steps are all done with `git config --global`:

1. Make your name known to Git,
   since it will be recorded in every commit you make ---
   your actual first and last name (***not** your OSC or GitHub username!*):

   ```sh
   git config --global user.name 'John Doe'
   ```

2. Make your email address known
   (_should match the address associated with your GitHub account,_
   _if you already created one_):

   ```sh
   git config --global user.email 'doe.391@osu.edu'
   ```

3. Set a default text editor for Git.
   (Git may occasionally open a text editor for you.
   Even though we're using VS Code,
   here it is better to select a text editor that runs in the shell, like `nano`^[
   Git will open an editor when you need to provide a "commit message" but didn't
   enter one on the command line.
   Its default editor is `vi`/`vim`, which is more complicated and,
   for example, notoriously hard to exit for beginners.].)

   ```sh
   git config --global core.editor "nano -w"
   ```

4. Change the default "branch" name to `main`
   (Git's default is still the older `master`, whereas GitHub uses `main`):

   ```sh
   git config --global init.defaultbranch main
   ```

5. Finally, check whether you successfully changed the settings:

   ```sh
   git config --global --list
   ```
   ```bash-out
   user.name=John Doe
   user.email=doe.391@osu.edu
   core.editor=nano -w
   init.defaultbranch=main
   ```

## Your first Git repository

You'll create a Git repository for a **mock book project**:
writing Charles Darwin's "On the Origin of Species".
This example follows Chapter 2 of @allesina2019 and it's another example you may
find silly,
but it will help you learn the basic Git workflow while writing content that is
easy to understand.

### Start a new Git repository

Create a new dir for a mock project that you will version-control with Git,
and navigate there:

``` sh
# (Your starting point should be /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER/week05)
mkdir originspecies
cd originspecies
```

The command to **initialize a new Git repository is `git init`** ---
use that to start a repo for the `originspecies` dir:

``` sh
git init
```
``` bash-out
Initialized empty Git repository in /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/jelmer/week05/originspecies/.git/
```

Can we confirm that the Git repo dir is there?
Recall from the previous lecture that Git stores its data in a **hidden dir called**
`.git`. We can use the `ls` command with the `-a` option to show hidden files and dirs:

```bash
# (ls -a will also show the current dir "." and the parent dir "..")
ls -a
```
```bash-out
.  ..  .git
```

Next, check the status of your new repository with `git status`:

``` sh
git status
```

``` bash-out
On branch main

No commits yet

nothing to commit (create/copy files and use "git add" to track)
```

Git reports that you:

- Are on a "branch" called `main`.
  We won't cover Git branches in class, but this is discussed in the
  [optional self-study material](../bonus/git.qmd) and @allesina2019 Chapter 2.6.
  Basically, branches are "parallel versions" of your repository.

- Have not created any commits yet.

- Have "nothing to commit" because there are no files in this dir.

### Your first Git commit

You will start writing the book ([😉]{style="font-size:1.2em"})
by `echo`-ing some text into a new file called `origin.txt`:

``` sh
echo "An Abstract of an Essay on ..." > origin.txt
```

Now, check the status of the repository again:

``` sh
git status
```
<pre class="bash-out"><code>On branch main

No commits yet

Untracked files:
  (use "git add &lt;file&gt;..." to include in what will be committed)
        <span class="git-red">origin.txt</span>

nothing added to commit but untracked files present (use "git add" to track)</code></pre>

Git has clearly **detected** the new file.
But as mentioned in the intro slides, Git does not automatically start "tracking" files ---
that is, it won't automatically include all files that are in your dir in the repository.
Instead, it tells you the file is "Untracked" and gives a hint on how to add it to the repository.

So, **start tracking the file and stage it all at once** with `git add`:

``` sh
# (Note that tab-completion on file names will work here, too)
git add origin.txt
```

Check the status of the repo again:

``` sh
git status
```
<pre class="bash-out"><code>On branch main

No commits yet

Changes to be committed:
  (use "git rm --cached &lt;file&gt;..." to unstage)
        <span class="git-green">new file:   origin.txt</span></code></pre>

Now, your file has been added to the **staging area** (also called the **Index**)
and is listed as a "_change to be committed_"^[
You also get a hint on how to "*unstage*" the file:
i.e., reverting what you just did with `git add` and leaving the file untracked once again].
That phrase means that if you now run `git commit`,
the file will be included in that commit.

So, with your file tracked & staged, let's make your **first commit**.
Add the option `-m` followed by a "**commit message**":
a short description of the changes you are including in the current commit^[
If you leave out `-m`, Git will instead open the `nano` editor that you
configured above, so you can type your commit message there.]:

``` sh
git commit -m "Started the book"
```

``` bash-out
[main (root-commit) 3df4361] Started the book
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
 create mode 100644 origin.txt
```

You've made your first commit!
Here is another way of visualizing the adding and committing of changes in Git:

![](../img/git-do1.png){fig-align="center" width="48%" fig-alt="A diagram of the process of adding and committing changes with Git commands" .lightbox}

::: legend2
Note that `git add` has a dual function: it starts tracking files and stages them.
:::

Let's check the status of the repo again:

``` sh
git status
```

``` bash-out
On branch main
nothing to commit, working tree clean
```

It reported "nothing to commit, working tree clean",
which means no changes have been made since the last commit.
TODO - explain "working tree" (cf "working dir")

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
Try to get in the habit of using `git status` a lot ---
as a sanity check before and after other `git` actions.
:::

Also look at the **commit history** of the repo with `git log`:

``` sh
git log
```

<pre class="bash-out"><code><span class="git-yellow">commit 3df4361c1de9b71e08bf6e050105d53097acec21</span> (<span class="git-cyan git-bold">HEAD</span> -&gt; <span class="git-green git-bold">main</span>)
Author: Jelmer Poelstra &lt;jelmerpoelstra@gmail.com&gt;
Date:   Mon Mar 11 10:55:35 2024 -0400

    Started the book</code></pre>

Note the "hexadecimal code" (which uses numbers and the letters `a`–`f`)
on the first line ---
this is a unique identifier for each commit, called the **SHA-1 checksum**.
You can reference and access each past commit with these checksums.

::: exercise

cd myproject

Which ones?

<!---
<details><summary> {{< fa check-circle >}} _Click for the solution._ </summary>

</details>

:::

### Your second commit

Start by modifying the book file --- you'll actually overwrite the earlier content:

``` sh
echo "On the Origin of Species" > origin.txt
```

Check the status of the repo:

``` sh
git status
```

<pre class="bash-out"><code>Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git add &lt;file&gt;..." to update what will be committed)
  (use "git restore &lt;file&gt;..." to discard changes in working directory)
        <span class="git-red">modified:   origin.txt</span>

no changes added to commit (use "git add" and/or "git commit -a")</code></pre>

Git has **noticed** the changes, because the file is being tracked:
`origin.txt` is listed as "modified".

But changes to tracked files are **not** automatically staged ---
use `git add` to **stage** the file as a first step to committing these changes:

``` sh
git add origin.txt
```

::: {.callout-tip}
#### Git never acts on files by itself
Git behaves similarly when it comes to new files and changes to tracked files:
it does not automatically do anything with them.
That is deliberate: managing which files are tracked and staged is up to you.
:::

Now, make your second commit, again adding a commit message.
Like always, you can decide what to write,
but the idea is that you give a short description of the changes you made:

``` sh
git commit -m "Changed the title as suggested by Murray"
```

``` bash-out
[main f106353] Changed the title as suggested by Murray
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+), 1 deletion(-)
```

Git gives a brief summary of the changes that were made:
you changed 1 file (`origin.txt`), and since you replaced the line of text in that file,
it interprets that as 1 insertion (the new line) and 1 deletion (the replaced line).

Check the history of the repo again --- you'll see that there are now 2 commits:

``` bash
git log
```

<pre class="bash-out"><code><span class="git-yellow">commit f1063537b6a1e0d87d2d52c9e96c38694959997a</span> (<span class="git-cyan git-bold">HEAD</span> -&gt; <span class="git-green git-bold">main</span>)
Author: Jelmer Poelstra &lt;jelmerpoelstra@gmail.com&gt;
Date:   Mon Mar 11 11:01:49 2024 -0400

    Changed the title as suggested by Murray

<span class="git-yellow">commit 3df4361c1de9b71e08bf6e050105d53097acec21</span>
Author: Jelmer Poelstra &lt;jelmerpoelstra@gmail.com&gt;
Date:   Mon Mar 11 10:55:35 2024 -0400

    Started the book</code></pre>

As you start accumulating commits,
you might prefer `git log --oneline` for a one-line-per-commit summary:

```bash
git log --oneline
```
<pre class="bash-out"><code><span class="git-yellow">f106353</span> (<span class="git-cyan git-bold">HEAD</span> -&gt; <span class="git-green git-bold">main</span>) Changed the title as suggested by Murray
<span class="git-yellow">3df4361</span> Started the book</code></pre>

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
Once your history is longer than your screen,
`git log` opens in the `less` pager that you used last week:
scroll with the arrow keys and press <kbd>q</kbd> to get back to your prompt.
The same goes for long `git diff` output.
:::

::: callout-note
### Staging files efficiently

When you would like to stage multiple files, you don't need to add them one-by-one:

``` sh
# [Don't run any of this - these are hypothetical examples]
# Stage all files in the project/repository:
git add --all

# Stage all files in the current dir and its subdirs
# (from the repo's top-level dir, this is the same as 'git add --all'):
git add .

# Stage all files in a specific dir (here: 'scripts') in the project:
git add scripts/
```

Finally, you can use the `-a` option for `git commit` as a shortcut to
**stage and commit all changes** with a single command
(but this will not add untracked files!):

``` sh
# Stage & commit all changes to tracked files:
git commit -am "My commit message"
```
:::

### What to include in individual commits

The last example in the box above showed the `-a` option to `git commit`,
which allows you to stage and commit all changes to tracked files at once.
That seems more convenient than separately `git add`ing files before committing.

However, rather than committing everything at once (say, at the end of each day),
it's good practice to make each commit a unit of progress worth saving ---
and as such, to **create separate commits for distinct changes**.
For example, say you use `git status` to check which files you've changed
since your last commit, and you find that you have:

- Updated a README file to include more information about your samples.
- Worked on a script to run quality control of sequence files.

These are completely unrelated changes,
and it's **not** recommended to include both in a single commit.

::: exercise
#### {{< fa user-edit >}} Exercise 2: Separate commits

_TODO - improve this exercises -- too confusing/ advanced to have unrelated edits in one file here_

Say that since your last commit, you have:

1. Added sample information to `README.md`.
2. Changed the output dir in `scripts/qc.sh` from `qc` to `results/qc`.
3. Updated the line in `README.md` that describes where the QC output goes.

How many commits would you make, and which change(s) would go in each?

<!----
<details><summary> {{< fa check-circle >}} _Click for the solution._ </summary>

Two commits: one for change 1, and one for changes 2 and 3 together.
Changes 2 and 3 are in different files, but they form a single unit of progress:
the README should match what the script does.
So, the rule is "one commit per change", not "one commit per file".
</details>
---->

Bonus: can you make these commits with the commands you know so far?

<!----
<details><summary> {{< fa check-circle >}} _Click for the solution._ </summary>

and `git add README.md` stages the whole file,
so you can't split these changes up this way.
(It is possible, though: VS Code lets you stage selected lines,
and on the command line, you can use `git add -p`.)
</details>
---->

:::

_Below, we'll go through a few related key aspects of using Git._

## Ignoring files and directories

As discussed in the [intro slides](./w5a_git-intro.qmd#what-to-version-control),
it's best not to track some files,
such as (bulky) data files, temporary files, and results.
We've seen that Git reports any "untracked" files in your project whenever you
run `git status`. This can get annoying and make it harder to spot changes and
untracked files that you do want to add ---
and you might even **accidentally start tracking** these files,
for example with `git add --all`.

To deal with this, you can **tell Git not to pay attention to certain files** by adding
file names and wildcard selections to a special file called `.gitignore`.

To see this in action,
start by adding some content that you don't want to commit to your repository:
a dir `data`, and a file ending in a `~`
(a temporary file type that e.g. text editors can produce):

``` sh
mkdir data
touch data/drawings_1855-{01..12} todo.txt~
```

When you check the status of the repo, you see that Git has noticed these files:

``` sh
git status
```

<pre class="bash-out"><code>Untracked files:
  (use "git add &lt;file&gt;..." to include in what will be committed)
        <span class="git-red">data/</span>
        <span class="git-red">todo.txt~</span></code></pre>

If you don't do anything about this,
Git will keep reporting these untracked files whenever you run `git status`.
**To prevent this, you can create a `.gitignore` file:**

- The file should be called exactly `.gitignore`,
  and should be placed in the project's root dir.
- This is a plain text file that contains dir and file names/patterns,
  all of which will be ignored by Git.
- As soon as a `.gitignore` file exists,
  Git automatically checks and processes its contents.
- Perhaps somewhat counterintuitively,
  it's a good idea to add and commit this file to the Git repo.

Now, create a `.gitignore` file and add entries to instruct Git
to ignore everything in the `data/` dir, and any file that ends in a `~`:

``` sh
# Ignore everything in the data dir:
echo "data/" > .gitignore
# Ignore everything that ends in a ~:
echo "*~" >> .gitignore
```
```sh
cat .gitignore
```
```bash-out
data/
*~
```

When you check the status again,
Git will have automatically processed the `.gitignore` file,
and the targeted files should no longer be listed as untracked files:

``` sh
git status
```

<pre class="bash-out"><code>Untracked files:
  (use "git add &lt;file&gt;..." to include in what will be committed)
        <span class="git-red">.gitignore</span></code></pre>

However, you do now have an untracked `.gitignore` file,
so track and commit this file as follows:

``` sh
git add .gitignore
git commit -m "Add a gitignore file"
```

``` bash-out
[main 9715ab5] Add a gitignore file
 1 file changed, 2 insertions(+)
 create mode 100644 .gitignore
```

::: exercise
#### {{< fa user-edit >}} Exercise 4: `.gitignore`

1. Say that a repo's `.gitignore` file contains these two lines:

   ```bash-out-solo
   results/
   *.log
   ```

   Which of these new files would Git _not_ ignore?

   a) `results/counts.tsv`
   b) `run.log`
   c) `scripts/run.log`
   d) `scripts/qc.sh`

   <!----
   <details><summary> {{< fa check-circle >}} _Click for the solution._ </summary>

   Only **d)**.
   `results/counts.tsv` is inside an ignored dir, and both `.log` files match `*.log`.
   Note that c) is ignored too: patterns like `*.log` (and `results/`, too)
   match in any dir of the repo, not just in the top-level dir.
   </details>
   ---->

2. Say that you add the line `todo.txt` to the `.gitignore` file of your `originspecies` repo,
   and then append another line to `todo.txt`.
   Would `git status` report that `todo.txt` was modified?

   <!----
   <details><summary> {{< fa check-circle >}} _Click for the solution._ </summary>

   Yes: `.gitignore` only affects _untracked_ files.
   Because `todo.txt` is already tracked (you committed it in Exercise 4),
   Git keeps tracking it and reports changes to it.
   To stop tracking a file, you'd first have to remove it from the repo,
   as shown in the [optional self-study material](../bonus/git.qmd).
   </details>
   ---->
:::

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

::: callout-tip
### Good project file organization makes ignoring files easy

If you keep your data and results in their own top-level dirs, as recommended in week 2,
the two lines `data/` and `results/` in your `.gitignore` file are all you need to ignore them.
If you instead mix, for example, scripts and results within dirs,
you'll need many more specific and error-prone `.gitignore` entries.
:::

## File states and showing changes

### File states

To formalize what we've seen earlier,
tracked files can be in one of three states:

- Unchanged since the last commit: **committed** (=> latest version is in the repo/commits).
- Modified and staged since the last commit: **staged** (=> latest version is in the stage/"Index").
- Modified but not staged since the last commit: **modified** (=> latest version is in the working tree).

::: exercise
#### {{< fa user-edit >}} Self-study exercise: File states

Say that in a different repo, `git status` prints the following:

<pre class="bash-out-solo"><code>On branch main
Changes to be committed:
  (use "git restore --staged &lt;file&gt;..." to unstage)
        <span class="git-green">modified:   scripts/qc.sh</span>

Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git add &lt;file&gt;..." to update what will be committed)
  (use "git restore &lt;file&gt;..." to discard changes in working directory)
        <span class="git-red">modified:   README.md</span>

Untracked files:
  (use "git add &lt;file&gt;..." to include in what will be committed)
        <span class="git-red">scripts/trim.sh</span></code></pre>

1. Which file(s) would be included in a commit if you now ran `git commit -m "My message"`?

   a) Only `scripts/qc.sh`
   b) `scripts/qc.sh` and `README.md`
   c) All three files
   d) None of them: you first need to run `git add`

   <details><summary> {{< fa check-circle >}} _Click for the solution._ </summary>

   The correct answer is **a)**.
   Only _staged_ changes are included in a commit.
   `README.md` was modified but not staged,
   and `scripts/trim.sh` is not even tracked.
   </details>

2. And which file(s) would be included if you instead ran `git commit -am "My message"`?

   <details><summary> {{< fa check-circle >}} _Click for the solution._ </summary>

   `scripts/qc.sh` and `README.md`:
   the `-a` option stages all changes to _tracked_ files,
   but it does not add untracked files.
   </details>

3. Say that, instead, you edit `scripts/qc.sh` once more, without running `git add` again.
   How would `git status` list this file,
   and which version of it would `git commit -m "My message"` include?

   <details><summary> {{< fa check-circle >}} _Click for the solution._ </summary>

   `scripts/qc.sh` would be listed twice:
   under "Changes to be committed" _and_ under "Changes not staged for commit".
   `git add` stages the file as it was at that moment,
   so the commit would only include the earlier, staged changes.
   To also include your newest edits, run `git add` on the file again.
   </details>
:::

### Showing changes

The **`git diff` command** shows changes you have made to tracked files ---
by default, for each file, changes between:

- The **working tree** and the **last commit**, if you haven't staged the file.
- The **working tree** and the **stage (Index)**, if you have staged the file
  (so you'll only see changes that you made _after_ running `git add`).

Right now, there are no differences to report in our `originspecies` repository,
because your working tree, the stage/Index, and the last commit are all the same:

``` sh
# Git diff will not print anything if there are no changes to report:
git diff
```

Change the to-do list
(note: this will only work if you did the exercise above) and check again:

``` sh
echo "June 20, 1858: Send first draft to Huxley" >> todo.txt

git diff
```

<pre class="bash-out"><code><span class="git-bold">diff --git a/todo.txt b/todo.txt
index e3b5e55..9aca508 100644
--- a/todo.txt
+++ b/todo.txt</span>
<span class="git-cyan">@@ -1 +1,2 @@</span>
 June 18, 1858: read essay from Wallace
<span class="git-green">+June 20, 1858: Send first draft to Huxley</span></code></pre>

We won't go into the details of the above "diff format",
but at the bottom of the output above, you can see some specific changes:
the line "Send first draft to Huxley" was added (hence the **`+`** sign) in our
latest version of the file.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### More `git diff` *(Click to expand)*

- To show changes that you **have staged**
  (differences between the stage and the last commit),
  use the `--staged` option to `git diff`.
  So, don't be surprised if `git diff` shows nothing right after you ran `git add`!

- If you have changed multiple files, but just want to see differences for one
  of them, you can specify the filename to `git diff`.
  In our example, that prints the same output as the plain `git diff` command
  above, since we only changed one file:

  ```sh
  git diff todo.txt
  # Output not shown, same as above
  ```
:::

### VS Code functionality to show changes

VS Code has some built-in Git functionality,
some of which is quite a bit more user-friendly than the Git command-line interface.
For example, to see changes between files:

1. Click on the Git symbol in the narrow side bar (below the search icon)

2. In the source control sidebar,
   you should see the `garrigos` repository

   but you may not see the `originspecies` repository.
   If not, click "File" > "Open Folder" and select `week05/originspecies`
   to make VS Code start at that dir ---
   then, you should definitely see the `originspecies` repo.

3. Within the `originspecies` listing, you should see `todo.txt`:

![](../img/vscode_repos.png){fig-align="center" width="40%" fig-alt="A screenshot of the VS Code source control sidebar." .lightbox}

## Undoing changes that have not been committed

Here, you'll learn how to undo changes that have not been
committed, like undoing an accidental file removal or overwrite.
(In the [optional self-study Git material](../bonus/git.qmd),
you can learn how to unstage files and how to undo changes that _have_ been committed.)

### Recovering a version from the repo

We'll practice undoing changes to your working tree (that have not been staged)
by recovering a version from the repo: in other words,
using Git as an "undo button" after accidental file changes or removal.

First, commit the change you made to the to-do list above,
so that this latest version is stored in the repo:

``` sh
git commit -am "Add Huxley draft to to-do list"
```

Let's say you **accidentally overwrote** instead of appended to a file:

1. Accidental overwriting of the file [😳]{style="font-size: 1.2em;"}:

   ```sh
   echo "Finish taxidermy of the finches" > todo.txt
   ```

2. Next, always start by checking the status:

   ```sh
   git status
   ```
   <pre class="bash-out"><code>On branch main
   Changes not staged for commit:
     (use "git add &lt;file&gt;..." to update what will be committed)
     (use "git restore &lt;file&gt;..." to discard changes in working directory)
           <span class="git-red">modified:   todo.txt</span>

   no changes added to commit (use "git add" and/or "git commit -a")</code></pre>

3. You'll want to "discard changes in working directory",
   and Git told you how to do this --- with `git restore`:

   ```sh
   git restore todo.txt

   cat todo.txt
   ```
   ```bash-out
   June 18, 1858: read essay from Wallace
   June 20, 1858: Send first draft to Huxley
   ```

Great! You have successfully recovered the previous version of the file from the repo.

::: {.callout-warning}
#### `git restore` can only bring back what Git has stored
`git restore` replaces your file with the version stored by Git
(the last commit, or the staged version if you staged the file).
Had you not committed the Huxley line first, it would now be gone for good.
Keep in mind, too, that `git restore` itself _permanently_ discards any
uncommitted changes to the file --- one more reason to commit often!
:::

If you **accidentally deleted a file**,
you can similarly retrieve it with `git restore`:

1. Accidental removal of `todo.txt`

   ```sh
   rm todo.txt
   ```

2. Use `git restore` to get the file back!

   ```bash
   git restore todo.txt

   cat todo.txt
   ```
   ```bash-out
   June 18, 1858: read essay from Wallace
   June 20, 1858: Send first draft to Huxley
   ```

::: exercise
#### {{< fa user-edit >}} Exercise 5: What can Git restore?

In which of these situations can `git restore` **not** get back what you lost?

a) You accidentally overwrote a committed file, using `>` instead of `>>`.
b) You accidentally removed a committed file with `rm`.
c) You accidentally removed a new file that you had never added with `git add`.
d) You accidentally removed a whole dir of committed files with `rm -r`.
e) You accidentally overwrote a committed file, and want back the edits you had made to it
   since your last commit (without staging them).

<!----
<details><summary> {{< fa check-circle >}} _Click for the solution._ </summary>

The correct answers are **c)** and **e)**.
Git can only restore versions of files that it has stored.
It never stored anything for the file in c), nor for the uncommitted edits in e):
there, `git restore` would only give you the last committed version.
In the other cases, `git restore` will work ---
for d), you would run `git restore` followed by the name of the dir.
</details>
---->
:::

## A few Git best-practices

- **Write informative commit messages.**
  Imagine looking back at your project in a few months,
  after finding an error that you introduced a while ago.
  - Not-so-good commit message: "Updated file"
  - Good commit message: "In file x, updated function y to include z"

![By XKCD - [image source](https://xkcd.com/1296)](../img/xkcd-git-commit-msg.png){fig-align="center" width="70%" fig-alt="A humorous cartoon showing ever-worsening Git commit messages over time." .lightbox}

- **Commit often, using small commits.**\
  This will also help to keep commit messages informative!

- **Before committing, check what you've changed.**\
  Use `git diff [--staged]` or VS Code functionality.

- **Avoid including unrelated changes in commits.**\
  Separate commits if your working tree contains work from disparate edits:
  use `git add` + `git commit` separately for two sets of files.

- **Don't commit unnecessary files.**\
  These clutter your repo and its history
  (especially automatically generated, temporary files),
  and when collaborating, they can lead to so-called
  [merge conflicts](../bonus/git.qmd#merge-conflicts).
